idiom_name: @JvmInline value class + unit enum with conversion factors
implementation_notes: Kotlin's inline value classes are exactly the mechanism for this pattern: a value class with a single Double property is erased to the bare Double at runtime (no allocation, see the language docs on inline value classes) while the type still denotes the unit, so Length + Length is a real operation and Length + Time does not type-check. Pair it with an enum that holds each unit's factor to the dimension's base unit and expose companion factories such as Length.of(3.0, LengthUnit.KILOMETRE), keeping the constructor private so a raw number can never be wrapped in the wrong unit; operator functions (plus, compareTo) then give the value number-like ergonomics without operator overloading. For time, prefer the standard library: kotlin.time.Duration is the same idea implemented as an inline value class over a scaled Long.
pitfalls: Boxing comes back whenever a value class is used as a nullable, an interface implementation or a generic argument, so the zero-cost guarantee disappears exactly where the type is passed around; keep those seams rare.
A public constructor or a second factory taking a raw Double reopens the unit-less hole - the private constructor plus unit-taking factories is the invariant.
Double equality inside the value class means 1.0 km and 1000.0 m are unequal unless the factory normalises to a canonical unit; normalise, or document unit-sensitive equality.

variants.name: kotlin.time.Duration for time quantities
variants.implementation_notes: For durations the standard library already realises the pattern: Duration is an inline value class holding a scaled amount, the companion extension properties (500.milliseconds, 3.seconds, 2.days) construct values, arithmetic and comparison work across units, and inWholeHours / toDouble(DurationUnit) convert explicitly. DurationUnit covers nanoseconds to days, so a domain-specific type is only needed when the unit set must be data-driven or when the quantity is not time.
variants.code_sketch:
import kotlin.time.Duration
import kotlin.time.Duration.Companion.seconds
import kotlin.time.Duration.Companion.milliseconds
import kotlin.time.DurationUnit

val total: Duration = 3.seconds + 500.milliseconds
println(total.inWholeSeconds)                 // 3 (truncated)
println(total.toDouble(DurationUnit.SECONDS)) // 3.5
pitfalls: inWholeX properties truncate towards zero; use toDouble(unit) when the fractional part matters, and pick the larger unit only for display.
Duration saturates at Long limits rather than overflowing, so a huge product looks valid - it is clamped, not exact.
Nanosecond resolution on the JVM is limited by the platform clock; do not read Duration's precision as measured precision.

variants.name: JSR-385 javax.measure on the JVM
variants.implementation_notes: On the JVM the Java standard route is available from Kotlin too: javax.measure Quantity/Unit with Indriya, giving a data-driven unit catalogue, prefixes and the specification's rules for affine units. Choose it when units arrive from configuration, persistence or an external system, or when Java and Kotlin services must share the same unit model; the price is that dimension errors are runtime exceptions, not Kotlin type errors.
variants.code_sketch:
import tech.units.indriya.quantity.Quantities
import tech.units.indriya.unit.Units
import javax.measure.quantity.Length

val span = Quantities.getQuantity(3, Units.KILOMETRE)
val gap = Quantities.getQuantity(500, Units.METRE)
val total: javax.measure.Quantity<Length> = span.add(gap).to(Units.METRE)
pitfalls: Java generics erase into Kotlin as platform types, so a wrong dimension compiles and fails at run time with UnconvertibleException.
JSR-385 quantity values are only immutable by convention and BigDecimal equality is scale-sensitive, so compare with compareTo rather than ==.
